title: Why Two Identical Homes Can Cost Very Different Amounts to Design
excerpt: Same floor area, same building, wildly different project costs. Here is what actually drives the difference, and how to compare quotes fairly.
content:
Two apartments on the same floor of the same building. Same square footage. Same basic layout. One interior project costs Rs. 18 lakh. The other costs Rs. 36 lakh. Both results look good. Both clients are satisfied. The same design studio did both.

This is not unusual. Interior project costs for the same size of space can vary by a factor of two or three, and sometimes more, depending on a set of factors that have nothing to do with how large the home is. Understanding what actually drives the cost is useful both for setting realistic expectations and for making informed choices about where in your budget to put the emphasis.

Material specification: the single largest variable

Material choice drives more of the cost difference between two similar projects than any other factor. Consider floor finishes alone. A good-quality ceramic floor tile in a standard size costs roughly Rs. 40 to Rs. 80 per square foot. A large-format vitrified tile from a premium manufacturer costs Rs. 120 to Rs. 200 per square foot. Natural marble or imported stone can run Rs. 350 to Rs. 800 per square foot or more, depending on the variety and the finish. On a 1,200 square foot home, the difference between the lowest and highest floor option alone is Rs. 3.7 lakh to Rs. 8.6 lakh, before installation labour.

Multiply this logic across kitchen shutters, wardrobe finishes, wall treatments, ceiling materials, hardware, and sanitaryware, and the cumulative difference becomes very large. A home where every material decision is made at the premium tier is a fundamentally different cost proposition from one where mid-range materials are used throughout, even when the floor area is identical.

Joinery: standard versus custom

Kitchen cabinets, wardrobes, study units, and TV panels are among the most significant cost items in any interior project. The difference between standard modular joinery with laminate shutters and fully custom joinery with lacquered or veneered shutters, soft-close mechanisms, integrated handles, and bespoke heights and configurations is substantial. A modular kitchen for a medium-sized kitchen in India currently costs roughly Rs. 1.5 to Rs. 2.5 lakh. A fully custom kitchen in the same space with premium shutters, quartz or stone countertops, and designer hardware costs Rs. 4 to Rs. 8 lakh. Both are kitchens. The daily experience of using them is quite different.

False ceilings, lighting, and electrical

A basic gypsum false ceiling with standard downlights is a modest cost item. A layered false ceiling with cove lighting, integrated LED channels, step details, and a mix of accent and task lighting costs significantly more, both for materials and for the electrical work required to run and control it. Clients who want lighting flexibility, the ability to shift from a bright working light to soft ambient light with a switch, should budget for it specifically rather than expecting it to be included in a standard fit-out rate.

Site conditions that are invisible until the work starts

The condition of the existing space affects the cost of the new fit-out. A site with old plaster in poor condition, outdated electrical wiring that needs full replacement, or plumbing that requires significant re-routing costs more to bring to the standard required for a new interior than a structurally sound site with modern services. These costs are not always visible before the site is opened up, which is one reason a contingency buffer is important on every project.

Access also matters. A site in a high-rise building with a small lift requires smaller material deliveries and more trips, which adds time. A site in a gated community with restricted working hours has fewer productive hours per day. These factors affect execution cost rather than material cost, but they are real and they compound.

A side-by-side comparison: same size, different costs

Consider two 1,500 square foot homes. Home A uses standard laminate shutters throughout, ceramic flooring, a basic false ceiling with downlights, and mid-range sanitaryware. Total cost: approximately Rs. 1,200 per square foot, or Rs. 18 lakh. Home B uses lacquered shutters, large-format vitrified flooring, a layered false ceiling with cove lighting, stone countertops in the kitchen, and premium fixtures throughout. Total cost: approximately Rs. 2,400 per square foot, or Rs. 36 lakh. Same size. Double the cost. Very different results in the living of them.

How to compare two quotes fairly

If you receive two quotes for the same project and one is significantly lower than the other, the useful question is not why the expensive one is high, but what the cheaper one has excluded. Ask for a line-by-line material specification in both cases. Ask what grade of material is assumed for each item. Ask whether furniture is included or additional. Ask whether the professional fee is inside the quoted number or separate.

A quote that looks attractively low at the start of a project often reflects either a lower specification or a cost structure that will accumulate variation orders once work begins. Neither serves the client well. The most useful basis for comparison is a clear, detailed scope document on both sides, so you are comparing equivalent things.

If you have a quote you would like a second perspective on, or want to understand what the right budget looks like for your project, speak to us at VOAD. We are happy to have that conversation before you make any commitment.
author: Ar. Vivek Bosmiya

title: How Long Does a Home Design Project Actually Take?
excerpt: Timeline is one of the most frequently misunderstood parts of any design project. Here is a realistic breakdown, by project type, of what drives the duration and what you can do to keep it on track.
content:
Timeline is one of the most frequently asked questions in the first meeting, and one of the hardest to answer with a single confident number. The honest answer depends on the size and complexity of the project, the client's availability during the design phase, the lead times of specified materials, and the conditions of the site once work begins.

What we can offer is a realistic range for different project types and a clear explanation of what drives the time at each stage.

Interior fit-out: apartment or individual rooms

For a standard apartment interior fit-out, between 1,000 and 1,500 square feet in carpet area, with a clear brief and no structural changes, the realistic timeline from first meeting to handover is 14 to 20 weeks. The design phase, covering floor plans, 3D visualisations, material selection, and client approvals, takes 3 to 5 weeks at this scale. Civil and services work, including flooring, false ceiling, electrical modifications, and plumbing adjustments, takes 5 to 8 weeks on a well-managed site. Furniture procurement runs in parallel with the site phase when timing is planned correctly, but any piece with a long lead time needs to be ordered early. Final installation and styling takes 1 to 2 weeks.

This assumes a site that is ready for work when the contract begins, a client who is responsive during the design phase, and no significant surprises in the existing structure. Any one of these factors can extend the timeline.

Full home interior: larger residential projects

A complete interior fit-out for a larger home, 2,000 to 3,500 square feet, with more rooms, more custom joinery, and a more detailed brief, typically takes 20 to 32 weeks. The design phase extends to 5 to 8 weeks at this scale because there are more spaces to work through and more coordination decisions between areas. The site phase is longer because there is more work and more sequencing: some finishes cannot begin until others are complete, and a larger site has more potential for parallel workstreams to create scheduling pressure.

New construction: architecture plus interior design

A project that combines architectural design of a new building with interior design is measured in months, not weeks. For a residential bungalow in Gujarat, the architectural design phase, the building permit approval process, and the construction phase together typically span 18 to 30 months from first meeting to handover. Building permit approvals vary significantly by municipality. Some authorities process applications within 60 to 90 days; others take considerably longer. The construction timeline for a 3,000 to 4,000 square foot bungalow with a reliable contractor and no structural surprises is typically 12 to 18 months from approval to structural completion, with an additional 3 to 5 months for interior fit-out following that.

Planning around the Gujarat monsoon

If your project involves any external work, the Gujarat monsoon is a real scheduling consideration. Rajkot typically receives most of its annual rainfall between late June and mid-September. Exterior plastering, painting, waterproofing, and landscape work all slow significantly during heavy monsoon weeks. A good studio will plan the site schedule to complete external work before June or after September, and to use the monsoon period for internal work that is not affected by rain. For new construction projects beginning in the first quarter of a year, this often means pushing to close the structural shell before June so that interior work can continue through monsoon without major disruption.

What the client can do to keep the project on track

The single biggest factor in whether a project finishes on its original timeline is client responsiveness during the design phase. Respond to design queries within 24 to 48 hours. Visit material showrooms in person rather than approving samples from a photograph when a significant material choice is involved. Make decisions in sequence rather than revisiting earlier choices repeatedly. Communicate any budget changes as soon as they become apparent rather than mid-procurement.

A client who is engaged and decisive during the design phase is the most reliable contributor to a construction phase that runs smoothly and a handover date that holds. The construction phase has its own momentum; the design phase is where time is most within the client's control.

The questions to ask in your first meeting

When you meet a design studio for the first time, ask these things about timeline: What is the realistic duration for a project of this scope, not the optimistic version? What are the most common causes of delay on projects like this? What happens to the timeline if I need to make a significant change during construction? If the project begins in a specific month, when should I realistically plan to be living in the finished space?

A studio that answers these questions with a single confident number may be giving you the answer they think you want to hear. A studio that answers with a range and an honest explanation of what could affect it at each end is one that has managed enough projects to know that honesty at the start produces better outcomes for everyone. If you are planning a project and want to understand the realistic timeline for your specific scope, reach out to us at VOAD. We can give you an accurate picture once we understand the brief.
author: Ar. Vivek Bosmiya

title: What Nobody Tells You Before You Start a Turnkey Interior Project
excerpt: Turnkey sounds simple. Hand over the brief, collect your keys. The reality between those two moments has specific demands on the client that most studios do not spell out clearly enough.
content:
The word turnkey makes a project sound simpler than it is. Hand over the brief, we will handle everything, collect your keys when it is done. That is the promise, and in broad terms it is accurate. But between the brief and the keys is a process with specific demands on the client, specific risks, and specific moments where things can go slower than anyone planned.

After years of managing turnkey interior projects, here is what we tell clients at the very start of an engagement, rather than waiting for them to discover it mid-project.

The biggest cause of delays is not the contractor

On a well-managed project, contractors are not the primary source of delays. The primary source is client decision-making. Every time a material choice, a colour, a layout, or a specification needs approval, and that approval takes days rather than hours, the project waits. This is not a criticism: life gets busy, and some decisions genuinely take time to think through. But it is the reality of how projects slow down in practice.

The fastest projects we have managed are ones where clients were responsive during the design phase, made clear decisions when presented with options, and trusted the studio on technical matters that fell within the agreed brief. The slowest have been ones where every decision required extended family discussion or clients were unavailable at key moments. Your availability is one of the most important factors in your project's timeline.

Material lead times are real and non-negotiable

Certain materials have lead times that no studio can compress. Custom tiles from specific manufacturers: four to six weeks. Imported furniture or lighting fixtures: six to ten weeks. Bespoke joinery fabricated off-site: three to five weeks before it arrives for installation. If your brief includes any of these, the procurement process needs to begin well in advance of when that material is needed on site.

Changing a material choice after it has been ordered and is in transit is not simply a matter of making a different selection. It creates a gap in the site schedule, because the new material will have its own lead time, and it may result in additional costs if the original order cannot be cancelled or returned. The design phase exists precisely to make these decisions before procurement begins.

The site is never exactly what the drawings say

Every site has surprises. Old buildings especially. Walls that are not square. Electrical runs that are not where the drawings indicated. Plumbing that cannot be relocated without a more significant structural intervention. These discoveries happen on almost every project, and a good studio will have a clear process for managing them: document the issue, present the options to the client, agree on the path forward, continue. But each one requires a decision, and some of them have cost implications.

Building a contingency into your budget, typically 10 to 15 percent of the total project cost, is not pessimism. It is a practical acknowledgement that working with an existing built environment involves unknowns. A contingency that goes unspent is a pleasant outcome. A project without one that hits unexpected site conditions creates stress for everyone involved.

Site-ready has a specific meaning

Before interior fit-out can begin, the site needs to meet certain conditions. Structural work must be complete. The building must be weathertight. Electrical supply must be confirmed and working. Existing finishes to be removed must be cleared. If any of these conditions are not met when the interior team arrives, work cannot begin, and holding a contractor's team on a site that is not ready costs time and sometimes money.

If you are commissioning a turnkey interior fit-out in a newly constructed building, coordinate carefully with your builder to ensure the handover to the interior team happens in a condition that allows work to begin immediately. A two-week delay at the start of a site schedule has a way of compounding into a four-week delay at the end.

Changing your mind during construction has a real cost

Design changes during construction are significantly more expensive than making the right decision in the design phase. Changing a wall position after it has been built means demolition, re-construction, re-plastering, and re-finishing. Changing a kitchen layout after cabinetry has been fabricated means fabricating new pieces, and the original pieces typically cannot be returned. This is not unique to any particular studio; it is the economics of construction work everywhere.

The design phase exists to make every significant decision before site work begins. Read the drawings carefully. Ask questions about anything that is not clear. Visit material samples in person rather than approving them from a photograph when the choice matters. The time spent here pays back directly in a construction phase that runs without expensive reversals.

What makes a project go well

The clients whose projects go most smoothly are not necessarily the ones with the largest budgets or the simplest briefs. They are the ones who communicate quickly, who come to decisions with a clear sense of their priorities, who raise concerns directly rather than storing them, and who trust the studio on technical matters while staying genuinely engaged on the choices that shape the personality of their space. If you are considering a turnkey project and want to understand what the process actually looks like from the inside, get in touch with VOAD. We would rather set clear expectations at the start than manage difficult ones later.
author: Ar. Vivek Bosmiya

title: 5 Things to Know Before Hiring an Interior Designer in Rajkot
excerpt: Planning to hire an interior designer in Rajkot? Here is what every homeowner should know before signing a contract.
content:
Hiring an interior designer is one of the most significant decisions you make when building or renovating a home. In Rajkot, where the design market has grown rapidly over the last decade, knowing what to look for can save you time, money, and a great deal of frustration.

At VOAD Architecture & Interiors, we have worked with homeowners across Rajkot and Gujarat who came to us after difficult experiences with other studios. These five things are what they wish someone had told them first.

1. Portfolio speaks louder than promises

Any designer can present a beautiful mood board assembled from Pinterest. What matters is evidence of completed work: real projects, real spaces, real finishes. Ask to see a portfolio of completed projects similar in scale and style to what you have in mind. If a designer specialises in commercial interiors but you want a warm family home, that matters.

Pay attention to consistency. A designer whose work looks dramatically different across every project may lack a coherent design language, which can translate to an incoherent result for you. Look for a clear visual point of view across different project types and scales.

2. Understand exactly what the fee covers

Interior design fees in Rajkot are typically structured in one of three ways: a flat project fee, a percentage of the total project cost, or an hourly rate. Each has implications. A flat fee gives you certainty upfront. A percentage fee means the designer benefits financially from higher spending, which can create a subtle conflict of interest. An hourly rate can reward slow work.

More importantly, clarify what the fee does not include. Does it cover site visits? Procurement? Contractor coordination? Revisions beyond a certain number? Get this in writing before work begins. Ambiguity about fee scope is one of the most common sources of conflict between clients and designers in Gujarat.

3. Ask who will actually be working on your project

Many larger design firms sell on the strength of a senior designer's reputation and then hand the project to junior staff. You meet the principal at the pitch and rarely see them again. This is one reason we keep VOAD deliberately small: Ar. Vivek Bosmiya is the designer on every project, not a manager reviewing junior work. Whoever you hire, make sure you know who will be on site and who will be making day-to-day decisions.

4. Check references, not just website testimonials

Testimonials are curated. Ask for direct contact details of two or three previous clients and call them. Ask specific questions: Did the project finish on time? Was the final cost close to the estimate? Were there things the designer could have handled better? A confident designer will have no hesitation giving you references. If a studio is reluctant to connect you with past clients, treat that as meaningful information.

5. Clarify the timeline from the start

Interior projects in Rajkot routinely run over schedule, often because timelines were optimistic to begin with or because no single person was accountable for keeping contractors on track. Ask for a written project schedule with milestones, and ask how delays are communicated and managed.

A project that takes three months longer than planned is not a good result, regardless of how it looks at the end. Realistic timelines, shared in writing from the start, protect both sides.

6. Know what a realistic Rajkot interior project costs

Interior design costs in Rajkot vary widely depending on scope and specification. A basic bedroom or living room fit-out by a competent local contractor may run between Rs. 800 and Rs. 1,500 per square foot for materials and labour. A mid-range residential project managed by a professional design studio typically falls between Rs. 1,500 and Rs. 2,500 per square foot. High-specification work with custom joinery, imported materials, or extensive false ceiling treatments can go considerably higher.

These figures cover materials and execution and do not include the designer's professional fee, which is usually charged separately. Being honest about your budget from the first meeting allows a designer to tell you clearly whether your expectations are achievable for what you want to build. A good designer will not take on a project whose budget cannot support the quality you have in mind. A clear budget conversation at the start saves time for everyone involved.

7. Look for local material knowledge

Gujarat has a strong tradition of craft and material production. Rajkot and the surrounding region offer access to local stone, handmade tiles, skilled woodworkers, and a network of craftsmen with deep trade experience. A designer with genuine local knowledge can source these materials thoughtfully and use them in ways that suit both the design vision and the Gujarat climate.

Ask any designer you are considering how familiar they are with local sourcing across Rajkot and Ahmedabad. A studio that relies entirely on branded showrooms and national catalogues may be missing the most interesting and cost-effective options available locally. The best residential interiors in Gujarat almost always combine national-quality design thinking with materials and craft that are rooted in the region.

If you are planning an interior project in Rajkot or Gujarat and would like to discuss your space, get in touch with us. We are happy to answer questions before you commit to anything.

title: How to Restore a Heritage Haveli in Gujarat
excerpt: Heritage havelis across Gujarat are slowly disappearing, not for lack of resources but for lack of the right approach. Here is what restoration actually involves.
content:
Gujarat has a remarkable built heritage. From the ornate havelis of Kutch to the step-well architecture of Patan, the state contains some of the finest examples of traditional Indian craftsmanship. Yet far too many of these buildings are quietly falling apart, not for lack of resources but for lack of the right approach.

Restoring a heritage haveli is fundamentally different from renovating a modern home. The decisions you make in the first few weeks set the course for everything that follows. Treating a heritage structure like a standard renovation project is the most common mistake owners make, and it is one that is very difficult to undo.

Start with a structural assessment

Before any restoration work begins, a qualified structural engineer must assess the building. Heritage structures often use load-bearing walls, lime mortar, and timber frames that behave very differently from modern reinforced concrete. Cracks that look alarming may be superficial. Sections that look intact may be significantly compromised. You need a professional assessment, not a visual guess from a contractor who primarily builds new construction.

Document everything before you touch it

Photograph and measure every element of the original structure before any intervention. Original jaali work, carved brackets, hand-painted plasterwork, stone thresholds: these details are irreplaceable once lost. Documentation also gives you a reference point if restoration work needs to be halted and resumed later, which is common on larger properties. A complete photographic and measured record costs very little relative to what it protects.

Work with conservation-aware architects

Not every architect has experience with heritage structures. Look for professionals who understand traditional construction techniques, are familiar with Gujarat-specific materials like Dhrangadhra stone and lime-pozzolana plasters, and have worked on projects reviewed by heritage bodies. At VOAD, heritage design is one of our core specialisations, and we approach every heritage project with the same documentation-first discipline. The wrong architect can cause more damage in two months than decades of neglect.

Respect the original materials

The single most common mistake in heritage restoration is replacing traditional materials with modern substitutes. Lime plaster gets replaced with cement. Teak joinery gets replaced with aluminium. Hand-carved stone gets replaced with cast concrete replicas. These substitutions look wrong, perform badly in the same climate the original materials were designed for, and can cause long-term structural damage by trapping moisture in ways lime construction was never meant to handle. Source period-appropriate materials even when they are harder to find and more expensive to use.

Navigate heritage regulations early

If the structure is listed or sits in a heritage zone, you will need approvals before any modification. The process in Gujarat can take time, particularly for structures under ASI or state heritage board jurisdiction. Start this paperwork as early as possible, ideally before you have committed to a contractor or a timeline. Your architect should know which permissions apply to your specific property and how long the approval process typically takes in that jurisdiction.

Understand what restoration costs in Gujarat

Heritage restoration is typically more expensive per square foot than new construction, and the range is wide. A basic structural stabilisation and waterproofing project on a small haveli in Gujarat may start at Rs. 1,200 per square foot. A full restoration that involves carved stone repair, lime plaster reinstatement, and custom woodwork to match the original can reach Rs. 3,000 to Rs. 5,000 per square foot or more, depending on the extent of craft detail and the availability of craftsmen skilled in the specific techniques required.

The cost is driven heavily by the condition of the structure, the extent of missing or damaged original material, and the scarcity of the skills involved. Get a detailed scope and cost estimate from your architect before committing to a timeline. Surprises are common in restoration work; a well-prepared estimate will include a contingency for the unexpected, typically 15 to 20 percent of the project cost.

Plan for ongoing maintenance

Heritage buildings require long-term care. The restoration process is not a one-time event after which the building takes care of itself. Lime plasterwork needs periodic attention. Timber frames require protection from humidity and seasonal pests. Roofs need inspection and repointing after each monsoon season in Gujarat, where rainfall can be intense and concentrated.

The most successful heritage restorations we have seen across Gujarat are those where the owners commit to a maintenance plan from the start, rather than treating restoration as a renovation that, once complete, requires nothing further. A well-maintained restored haveli can serve as a family home, a heritage stay, a cultural space, or a combination of uses for generations. The investment in careful restoration pays back in durability and character in a way no new construction can replicate.

If you are considering the restoration of a heritage property in Gujarat and want to understand what the process looks like for your specific building, contact VOAD. We are glad to discuss scope and complexity before you take on any commitment.
author: Ar. Vivek Bosmiya

title: Bungalow vs Villa: What Suits the Gujarat Climate?
excerpt: Gujarat's heat, monsoon, and mild winters demand architectural respect. Choosing the right home form affects how comfortable and costly your home is to live in.
content:
One of the most common questions we hear from clients planning a new home in Rajkot is whether to build a bungalow or a villa. The answer is rarely about budget alone. It depends on the site, the family, and most importantly, the climate.

Gujarat has a climate that demands architectural respect. Summers regularly exceed 42 degrees Celsius in Rajkot. Monsoon brings intense but concentrated rainfall between June and September. Winters are mild but occasionally cool at night. The right design choice significantly affects how comfortable and how costly your home is to live in year-round, and the difference compounds over decades.

What defines each type

In Gujarat's residential market, a bungalow typically refers to a ground-floor or single-storey home with a private plot, garden, and car parking. A villa more often describes a two or three-storey home on a standalone plot or within a gated compound, usually with a contemporary facade and more vertical floor planning. These terms are used loosely by developers and agents in Rajkot, so clarify with your architect exactly what you mean when you use either word.

How bungalows perform in Gujarat's climate

A well-designed bungalow handles the Gujarat climate more naturally. The single storey allows for a wide roof overhang, which shades the walls and windows during peak summer. Cross-ventilation is easier to achieve when the entire living area is on one level. Courtyard-style bungalows, common in traditional Gujarati home design, create natural cooling through convection and shade interior spaces that would otherwise bake in direct sun. On large plots in established Rajkot neighbourhoods, the bungalow form is often the more thermally comfortable choice, particularly for families who spend significant time at home during the day.

How villas perform in Gujarat's climate

Multi-storey villas concentrate more living area on a smaller footprint, which is an advantage on smaller urban plots in central Rajkot where land is expensive. However, upper floors accumulate more heat in summer unless the design specifically addresses solar gain through insulated roofs, recessed windows, double-glazed western facades, or strategic vegetation on the building perimeter. A villa designed without careful attention to Gujarat's climate will require more mechanical cooling, which means higher electricity costs throughout a long summer. The upper-floor bedroom that seemed like a luxury in the showroom becomes a liability at 2 am in April.

What matters most: orientation and materials

Regardless of form, orientation and material selection matter more than building type. A home with its main living areas facing west in Rajkot will struggle in summer regardless of whether it is a bungalow or villa. Light-coloured exterior finishes, thick wall construction, double glazing on western facades, and adequate roof insulation make a measurable difference to interior temperatures across the year. See our project portfolio for examples of how we address these factors across both building types and a range of plot orientations in Rajkot.

Typical plot sizes and costs in Rajkot

In Rajkot's established residential neighbourhoods, bungalow plots commonly range from 200 to 500 square yards. A well-designed bungalow on a 300 square yard plot can comfortably accommodate four bedrooms, generous living and dining areas, a garden, and covered parking. Construction costs for a good-quality bungalow in Rajkot typically start at around Rs. 1,800 to Rs. 2,500 per square foot for structure and standard finishes, with premium interiors and landscape adding to this figure.

Villa developments in Rajkot are more common in planned townships and gated communities on the city's outskirts, where plots are standardised and community infrastructure such as security and landscaping is shared. The compact footprint of a villa makes better use of a smaller plot in a premium location, though upper-floor living requires careful attention to the thermal management considerations described above. Get an independent cost estimate before committing to a developer's quoted rate.

The architect's role in climate performance

The difference between a home that stays comfortable without constant air conditioning and one that demands it from April to October almost always comes down to decisions made at the design stage. Wall thickness, window placement and size, roof insulation specification, shading devices, and the position of service spaces relative to living areas are all far cheaper to get right from the start than to retrofit later. If you are building a new home in Rajkot, invest time early in understanding how the building will perform thermally across Gujarat's seasons, not only how it will look in a render.

Making the right choice for your family

A family that wants ground-floor living for elderly members and young children will find a bungalow more practical. A family prioritising a compact footprint, a private upper-level primary suite, or a specific gated community will find a villa layout more appropriate. The best answer depends on your specific plot, family size, and how you intend to use the space day to day across all seasons.

If you are at the planning stage and want to discuss which form suits your plot and lifestyle, get in touch with VOAD. We work across both building types and have completed projects in Rajkot and across Gujarat.

title: What Does a Turnkey Interior Project Actually Include?
excerpt: The word turnkey gets used loosely in the design industry. Here is exactly what it means at VOAD and what you should expect from any studio that offers it.
content:
The word turnkey gets used loosely in the design and construction industry. Some firms use it to mean they will coordinate the contractors. Others mean they handle everything from the initial design sketch to the day you receive the keys. The difference matters enormously when you are planning a project and comparing studios in Rajkot or across Gujarat.

At VOAD Architecture & Interiors, turnkey means one thing: you hand over the brief and we handle everything until the space is ready to live or work in. Here is exactly what that covers.

Design and space planning

The process begins with a detailed brief and site measurement. We develop floor plans, elevation drawings, 3D visualisations, and material boards so you can see the complete vision before any work starts on site. Every change and approval happens at this stage, reducing the chance of expensive modifications during construction. Nothing begins on site until you have signed off on the design in full.

Material selection and procurement

We source and procure all materials: flooring, wall finishes, ceiling treatments, hardware, lighting fixtures, sanitaryware, and cabinetry. We work with suppliers across Rajkot, Ahmedabad, and nationally to find materials that suit both the design and the budget. You see the materials and samples before they are purchased. Nothing is ordered without your specific approval, and we maintain a full procurement log throughout the project.

Contractor coordination

We manage the civil and finishing contractors directly. This includes scheduling, site supervision, quality checks at each stage, and resolving the day-to-day problems that always arise on site. You do not need to visit the site daily or manage workers yourself. We are present on site so you do not have to be, and we provide regular updates so you always know where the project stands.

Furniture, furnishings, and styling

A turnkey project includes furniture selection and procurement: sofas, beds, dining tables, storage units, soft furnishings, and decor. We source pieces that are consistent with the design intent and the budget, not afterthoughts purchased from the nearest showroom. The final styling of the space, including the placement of objects and accessories, is part of the handover process. See completed examples of turnkey work across residential and commercial projects in our project portfolio.

The handover

When we hand over a turnkey project, the space is ready to use. We walk you through every system, fixture, and finish. We provide a snag list and return to address any items that need adjustment within an agreed period. The project is not considered complete until you are satisfied with every detail of the delivered space.

What a typical turnkey timeline looks like

A well-managed turnkey interior project in Rajkot for a three-bedroom home or apartment typically takes between 12 and 18 weeks from design sign-off to handover. A larger home or a more complex brief will take longer. The design phase, which includes drawings, 3D visualisations, material selection, and client approvals, usually accounts for 3 to 4 weeks. Civil work including flooring, false ceilings, electrical runs, and plumbing takes 5 to 8 weeks on a well-managed site. Furniture procurement, delivery, and final styling account for the remaining time.

Delays most commonly occur when client approvals are slow at key decision points, or when materials have long lead times from suppliers outside Rajkot. The fastest projects are always those where the client is available and decisive during the design phase. We provide a detailed project timeline at the start of every engagement so expectations on both sides are clear from the first week.

What turnkey does not include

It is equally important to be clear about what a turnkey interior contract does not cover. External landscaping and garden design, structural changes to the building such as adding rooms or removing load-bearing walls, and long-term maintenance services after handover are typically outside the scope of an interior turnkey contract. Appliances and home electronics are usually excluded unless specifically agreed and listed in the contract. If any of these are important to your project, discuss them before the contract is signed, not after work has started on site.

Is turnkey the right choice for your project?

Turnkey works best for clients who are time-constrained, based outside Rajkot during the project, or who simply prefer to delegate the full complexity of a build or fit-out to a professional team they trust. It is not always the right choice for clients who want to be directly involved in sourcing materials, visiting showrooms, or managing their own contractor relationships. A good studio will tell you honestly whether a turnkey contract suits your project and your working style, rather than recommending it as the default option for every client. Browse our completed turnkey projects to get a clear sense of the quality and scope you can expect from VOAD.

If you are considering a turnkey interior project in Rajkot or Gujarat and want to understand the timeline and investment involved, contact VOAD. We are happy to give you a realistic picture before you make any decision.
author: Ar. Vivek Bosmiya

title: What Does an Interior Design Project Actually Cost? A Realistic Guide
excerpt: The cost of an interior fit-out depends on far more than square footage. Here is an honest breakdown of pricing tiers, fee structures, and a worked example for a 3BHK in 2026.
content:
This is the question almost every client thinks about before they say it out loud. We appreciate that, and we prefer to address it openly. The cost of an interior design project is one of the areas where opacity does everyone a disservice: designers are reluctant to quote before they know the scope, clients are unsure what a reasonable expectation looks like, and the result is a first meeting where neither side has said what they actually mean.

Here is what interior design actually costs in India in 2026, with enough specificity to be genuinely useful.

The three tiers of interior finish

The cost of an interior fit-out is primarily driven by material specification. There are broadly three tiers, and most projects land somewhere within or between them.

Basic finish uses good-quality locally available materials: standard laminate shutters on kitchen and wardrobe units, ceramic or standard vitrified tile flooring, painted walls, and a simple false ceiling with standard fixtures. This tier is competent and can look clean and comfortable when designed well. Material and execution costs for a basic-tier fit-out in India currently range from approximately Rs. 900 to Rs. 1,400 per square foot, measured on the carpet area of the home.

Mid-range finish uses branded or higher-quality local materials: lacquered or membrane-pressed shutters, larger-format vitrified or natural stone flooring, wall panelling or textured finishes in at least some rooms, integrated LED lighting, custom or semi-custom joinery, and better-grade sanitaryware and hardware. This is the tier that most clients who want a finished, considered interior actually land in. Material and execution costs for mid-range finish range from approximately Rs. 1,600 to Rs. 2,500 per square foot.

Premium finish uses imported or specialist materials: marble or engineered stone surfaces, solid timber or high-quality veneer joinery, bespoke furniture, designer lighting fixtures, and a level of detail and craft that is visible in the finished result. Premium-tier interiors currently cost from approximately Rs. 2,800 to Rs. 4,500 per square foot, with very high-specification projects going higher still.

What the designer's fee looks like

The professional fee for interior design is typically charged separately from material and execution costs, and fee structures vary significantly between studios. Some charge a flat project fee: for a residential fit-out of 1,000 to 2,000 square feet, this typically ranges from Rs. 1 lakh to Rs. 3.5 lakh depending on the scope and complexity. Some charge a percentage of the total project cost, typically 10 to 15 percent. Some offer an all-in packaged rate per square foot that combines design, materials, and execution under one number.

Be clear about which structure applies before you sign anything. A percentage-based fee means the designer's income increases with higher material spending, which can create a subtle incentive toward more expensive options. A flat project fee gives you cost certainty on the design side regardless of material choices.

A worked example: 1,200 square foot 3BHK at mid-range

Materials and execution at Rs. 2,000 per square foot: Rs. 24 lakh. Designer's professional fee, charged as a flat project fee: Rs. 1.5 to Rs. 2.5 lakh. Furniture and furnishings, including sofas, beds, dining table, storage units, and soft furnishings: Rs. 3 to Rs. 5 lakh depending on brand choices. Lighting fixtures: Rs. 50,000 to Rs. 1 lakh. A 10 percent contingency buffer, which every project needs: Rs. 2.4 to Rs. 3.2 lakh.

Total realistic budget range for a 1,200 square foot, mid-range interior fit-out: approximately Rs. 31 to Rs. 36 lakh. The exact figure depends on material choices, the degree of custom joinery involved, and how much of the furniture budget goes toward branded versus locally sourced pieces.

Why two quotes for the same project can look very different

Two quotes for the same brief can differ significantly for legitimate reasons. One studio may include furniture procurement; another excludes it. One may use in-house execution teams; another outsources and applies a markup on contractor rates. One may specify higher-grade materials in their base quote; another presents a low opening number with a long list of additions once work begins.

When comparing quotes, ask what is specifically included and excluded in each. Ask to see a material specification, not just a per-square-foot rate. Ask whether the number is fixed or subject to change based on site conditions. The lowest initial quote is rarely the lowest final project cost.

The cost of getting design wrong

The most expensive interior projects are not always the highest-specified ones. They are the ones where design decisions were not made carefully at the start and had to be reversed during construction. Changing a floor plan after tiling has begun, replacing joinery that did not match the brief, re-running electrical points because the lighting layout was not thought through: each of these costs far more than getting the design right the first time.

The professional fee paid to a designer who asks the right questions, produces clear drawings, and supervises execution carefully is almost always worth more than it costs in time and avoided mistakes. If you would like a clear, honest conversation about budget for your specific project, get in touch with VOAD. We will tell you what we actually think before asking for any commitment from you.
author: Ar. Vivek Bosmiya

title: The Problem With Copying Interior Designs from Instagram
excerpt: Instagram is full of beautiful interiors. The problem starts when a photograph becomes a brief. Here is why copied designs rarely work, and what to do instead.
content:
We are not against Instagram. It is a genuinely useful place to gather visual references and understand what styles resonate with you. The problem is not the platform. The problem is what happens when a photograph becomes a brief.

Every week, clients come to us with saved images: a Scandinavian living room in muted tones with enormous floor-to-ceiling windows, a Mumbai penthouse with polished concrete and dramatic lighting, a New York loft with exposed brick and industrial steel. They are beautiful images, often photographed by professionals with significant lighting rigs, and they represent real spaces. The issue is that none of those contexts are the same as your context, and context is everything in interior design.

Photographs are optimised for the camera, not for living

Professional interior photography is a specific discipline with its own logic. Furniture is moved to create the best angle for the shot. Items necessary for daily life but visually messy, the router, the charging cables, the pile of shoes by the door, are removed or hidden. Wide-angle lenses make rooms look larger than they are. Lighting rigs positioned off-camera create a quality of light that rarely exists in the room under normal conditions.

When you respond to a photograph and feel it is exactly what you want, you are responding to a carefully constructed image, not to the experience of actually being in and living with that space. The two things are related but not the same.

Climate cannot be copied from a photograph

Interior design that works in Scandinavia, where daylight is precious and winters are long and dark, uses materials, colours, and window configurations calibrated for that specific climate. Large windows that beautifully flood a room with soft northern light in Oslo create solar heat gain and glare problems in a west-facing apartment during a Gujarat summer. Bare concrete floors that feel cool and sophisticated in a temperate European city feel cold and uninviting in a home where people typically sit and move around barefoot.

Gujarat's climate, with its intense heat from March through June, concentrated monsoon, and mild winters, shapes what materials and spatial configurations actually work in residential interiors here. Timber that performs beautifully in a humid coastal climate may warp or split in the drier conditions of the interior. Materials and finishes need to be chosen for where they will actually live, not where they were photographed.

Scale is invisible in photographs

A photograph gives no reliable information about the dimensions of a space. The beautiful minimal bedroom in the reference image may be 400 square feet. The bedroom you are designing is 150 square feet. The same furniture arrangement, the same palette, and the same proportions do not translate directly. Copying the look of a large space into a smaller one does not produce a smaller version of the same feeling. It produces something that feels cramped and confused.

Similarly, the context around a photographed interior shapes the design decisions that made it work in that place: the city, the building type, the street, the view from the windows, the quality of available natural light. Remove the context and many of those decisions stop making sense.

Materials in photographs are rarely what they appear to be

The warm, rich timber in the reference image may be genuine solid teak or it may be a printed laminate that photographs identically under studio lighting. The stone floor may be a large-format porcelain tile that mimics marble. The rough textured wall may be a specialist finish applied by a craftsman who spent three days on it. These distinctions matter enormously for what the space will feel like over time, and they are not visible in the photograph.

When clients ask us to reproduce a specific look from a reference image, the first question we ask is what the underlying material was and what would be appropriate to use in their specific home and climate. Often there is a good answer. Occasionally the look only works because of a material or a process that is either not practically available in India or not appropriate for the conditions of that particular project.

What reference images are actually good for

None of this means you should stop saving images. References are genuinely useful for communicating atmosphere: a palette range, a degree of formality or informality, a preference for natural materials versus lacquered finishes, a desired quality of light. They help a designer understand what direction you are drawn toward. The problem is treating them as a literal specification rather than as a starting point for a conversation.

The best version of this process is: you bring images that represent how you want the space to feel, and the designer interprets those feelings through the lens of your specific site, your climate, your budget, and the materials that are actually appropriate and available. The result is a space that is yours, informed by what you love in the references but designed for your actual life. That is a better outcome than a copy of something that was designed for someone else's context entirely. If you would like to explore what that process looks like for your home, speak to us at VOAD.
author: Ar. Vivek Bosmiya

title: Why Some Rooms Feel Right the Moment You Walk In
excerpt: There are rooms that stop you for a moment. You cannot say exactly why. The proportions, the light, the materials all seem to be in their proper relationship with each other. That feeling is not accidental.
content:
There is a room you walked into at some point, a hotel lobby, a friend's apartment, a building you visited once, that made you pause. You could not say exactly why it felt different. The proportions seemed correct. The light fell in a way that made the space calm rather than harsh. You could sense the quality of the materials without having to touch them. Everything felt as though it belonged together.

That feeling is not accidental, and it is not magic. It is the result of deliberate decisions made in design. Understanding what those decisions are does not diminish the experience. If anything, it makes the quality more interesting to think about.

Proportion: the thing that is hardest to explain and most felt

Proportion is the relationship between the dimensions of a space and the elements within it. A room with a ceiling height of 8 feet and a floor area of 400 square feet feels very different from the same floor area under a 10-foot ceiling. Not simply taller: fundamentally different in character. The vertical dimension changes how light behaves, how furniture reads against the wall, and how the body settles into the space.

The standard residential ceiling height in India, typically 10 to 10.5 feet, exists for practical and cost reasons. But within that constraint, decisions about where horizontal elements sit, the height of door frames, the level at which storage units stop, the depth of ceiling details or shadows, all shift the perceived proportion of a room significantly. A room where every horizontal element sits at exactly the same height tends to feel flat. A room with considered variation in the vertical plane feels composed and intentional.

Natural light: direction and quality matter more than quantity

More windows do not automatically mean more light, or at least not the kind of light that makes a room feel good. The direction a window faces, and the quality of light it admits, matters far more than the total number of openings. North light is consistent, soft, and even throughout the day. East light is warm and bright in the morning and disappears by afternoon. West light is harsh and hot in the evening, particularly in Gujarat during summer. South light is strong and directional.

A room that feels luminous on a slightly overcast day is often one where the window is positioned to admit diffused light from a consistent direction, rather than direct sun that creates glare and heat. The quality of light in a well-designed room is something you notice without being able to identify the source of your comfort. You are simply in a space that feels easy to be in.

Materials: warmth, texture, and what they communicate before you touch them

Materials speak before you touch them. A timber floor feels warmer underfoot, psychologically, than a stone floor of similar actual temperature. A rough-textured wall reads quieter than a smooth painted surface. Materials with visible grain, variation, or texture tend to feel more comfortable over time than materials that are perfectly uniform, because the eye finds something to rest on and settle into.

In our work at VOAD, we choose materials for how they age as much as for how they look at the moment of completion. A material that develops character over five years is preferable to one that looks perfect on handover day and begins to feel tired by year two. The stone and craft traditions of Gujarat offer materials that understand this: hand-cut local stone, natural timber, and lime-based finishes that shift subtly in character with light and humidity over time.

Furniture scale: the most commonly misjudged element

The scale of furniture relative to the room is one of the most common causes of spaces that look correct in a showroom and wrong at home. A large, deep sofa that feels generous on a 2,000 square foot showroom floor may overwhelm a 250 square foot living room completely. Furniture that is correctly scaled for a room allows the room itself to be present rather than disappearing behind the furniture.

We plan furniture layouts from the beginning of every project, not at the end. The placement, scale, and relationship of furniture to the room's dimensions is a design decision that happens alongside the floor plan. When furniture is considered early, rooms can be shaped and sized to hold the furniture in the right relationship, rather than furniture being chosen after the room is fixed and then struggling to fit.

The quality that is hardest to describe: coherence

The quality in a room that is hardest to pin down is coherence. A room where every element belongs to the same design language, where the materials, proportions, furniture, and lighting have all been chosen in relationship to each other, feels settled. The eye moves through the space without catching on elements that seem out of place.

Coherence is not the same as matching. A room where everything matches can feel monotonous and lifeless. Coherence is more like harmony than uniformity: different notes that resolve into something that makes sense together. It is the result of someone making choices in relation to each other rather than independently, and it is the core of what a good interior designer does. If you have a space in your home that has never quite felt right and you want to understand why, get in touch. Sometimes a single conversation is enough to see what is missing.
author: Ar. Vivek Bosmiya

title: How Much Space Does a Family Actually Need? The Numbers Behind a Good Home
excerpt: More square footage is not always better. Here is a practical, calculation-backed look at how much space a family of four genuinely needs to live comfortably.
content:
More space is not always better. This is one of the things that architectural training teaches quickly, and one of the things clients find hardest to believe when they are planning a new home. Larger rooms sound more desirable in theory. In practice, a room that is too large for its furniture and its use is often less comfortable than a smaller room that has been planned with care.

The question of how much space a family needs has a real answer, and it is worth understanding before you commit to a plot size, a floor plan, or a per-square-foot budget that you will live with for decades.

Understanding the numbers before you start

Before working out how much space you need, it is worth understanding which measurement you are actually working with. Carpet area is the usable floor area inside the walls of your home. Built-up area adds the thickness of the external walls, typically adding 10 to 15 percent to the carpet area figure. Super built-up area, common in apartment purchases in Gujarat and across India, adds a share of common areas like lobbies, corridors, and staircases, and typically runs 25 to 30 percent above the carpet area.

When planning a home, work in carpet area. When comparing apartment sizes quoted by developers, always ask for the carpet area figure before comparing. A 1,500 square foot super built-up apartment may have only 1,050 to 1,100 square feet of actual usable space inside.

Minimum comfortable room dimensions

These are guidelines based on how families actually live in rooms, not minimum code requirements. A master bedroom for a couple needs at least 150 square feet, roughly 12 by 13 feet, to comfortably fit a king bed, bedside tables, a wardrobe, and enough circulation space that you are not squeezing past furniture. Below 140 square feet, a master bedroom begins to feel crowded with standard furniture. A children's bedroom works at 100 to 120 square feet for a single child, or 140 square feet if two children will share the room.

A living room for a family of four needs roughly 200 to 250 square feet to accommodate a three-seat sofa, two armchairs, a centre table, and a media unit with enough clearance that the room does not feel like furniture storage. A combined living and dining area for four people works well at 320 to 380 square feet. A kitchen used regularly by one or two people is comfortable at 80 to 100 square feet. A family that cooks together and has multiple people in the kitchen at once needs 120 to 140 square feet at minimum.

A simple calculation for a family of four

Adding up the spaces above, a family of four needs approximately the following carpet area to live comfortably in a three-bedroom home: master bedroom at 160 square feet, two children's rooms at 110 square feet each, combined living and dining at 350 square feet, kitchen at 100 square feet, two bathrooms at 50 square feet each, one guest toilet at 25 square feet, and entrance area, passages, and internal wall space at approximately 160 square feet.

This totals roughly 1,075 square feet of carpet area. At a built-up area calculation of 15 percent above carpet area, that is approximately 1,235 square feet built-up for a comfortable three-bedroom home for four people. A 1,000 square foot built-up apartment for a family of four is livable but will require very efficient space planning and disciplined storage. A 1,500 square foot apartment gives the same family room to breathe, space for a guest occasionally, and spaces that feel uncrowded even when everyone is home together.

When larger is not better

A room significantly larger than the furniture and activity it holds often feels cold rather than generous. A living room of 500 square feet with a standard sofa and chairs has dead space that neither anchors the furniture nor serves any purpose. The skill in space planning is matching room size to room use, not maximising square footage for its own sake. We have seen 900 square foot apartments that feel entirely comfortable and well-organised for a couple, and 2,500 square foot homes that feel oddly disconnected because the rooms were sized for a different kind of life than the residents actually lead.

What good space planning does that square footage alone cannot

Efficient space planning creates usable storage within the floor area, so rooms can be smaller without feeling cluttered. It uses zoning to separate noisy activity areas from quiet sleeping zones without using excess corridor space as a buffer. It places rooms to maximise natural light and cross-ventilation, so smaller rooms feel more open than they measure. And it sequences the home so that moving from one area to another feels natural rather than effortful.

In Gujarat, where land costs and construction costs both make every square foot meaningful, the investment in careful space planning at the start of a project saves money and produces a home that works better, at any size. If you are trying to work out what floor area is right for your family and your budget, speak to us. We can help you think through the numbers before you commit to a plot or a floor plan.
author: Ar. Vivek Bosmiya

title: Vastu and Modern Design: How We Actually Work With Both
excerpt: Vastu comes up in nearly every client meeting in Gujarat. Here is our honest position on how to work with its principles thoughtfully without letting it override practical design decisions.
content:
If you are building or renovating a home in Gujarat, the question of Vastu will come up. It comes up in almost every client conversation we have. Grandparents raise it. Parents raise it. Sometimes the clients themselves ask, and sometimes they ask on behalf of a family member who will need to be reassured that the design respects certain principles before they can feel comfortable with it.

We have been asked this question enough times to have a clear position: Vastu and modern design are not in fundamental conflict. They require thoughtful handling, and occasionally they create real constraints. But in our experience, the core principles behind Vastu are remarkably compatible with what good architecture tries to do anyway. The challenge is separating the principles from the rigidity with which they are sometimes applied.

What Vastu is actually about

Vastu Shastra is an ancient Indian system of architecture and spatial arrangement that encodes relationships between a building and the natural environment: the sun, wind, water, and cardinal directions. At its core, it is about orientation and spatial organisation. Many of its guidelines, when read carefully, align closely with what good architects try to do regardless of tradition: orient the home to capture morning light in living areas, locate heavier service spaces on the south and west to buffer against heat, keep sleeping areas quieter and away from street-facing noise.

The principles become problematic when they are applied as a rigid checklist without regard for the specific plot, the local microclimate, or the family's actual pattern of use. A guideline that works perfectly for an east-facing plot in an open neighbourhood may be physically impossible on a narrow south-facing plot in a dense urban street. Good design, like thoughtful Vastu guidance, has to be responsive to the reality of the site it is working with.

How we handle Vastu in practice

In our studio, we engage with Vastu as a set of spatial principles to understand and work with, not a set of rules to apply mechanically. We begin by asking clients which aspects matter most to their family. For some, the placement of the pooja room is the central concern. For others, it is the orientation of the master bedroom, or the relationship between the main entrance and the kitchen. Understanding the priorities allows us to address what genuinely matters rather than attempting to satisfy every guideline simultaneously on a plot that may not permit it.

When there is a genuine conflict between a Vastu guideline and the practical design of the home, we discuss it openly. We explain what the guideline means in terms of the physical space, what accommodating it would require, and whether there is a design solution that honours the intent of the principle without compromising the functionality or comfort of the rest of the home.

The most common questions we get asked

Can I have an open kitchen with Vastu? The open kitchen is one of the most consistently requested features in contemporary residential design. Traditional Vastu guidelines suggest the kitchen should be a separate, enclosed space, typically in the south-east corner of the home. In practice, many clients choose a semi-open kitchen with a visual screen or partial wall that provides the openness they want while preserving some spatial separation. This is a design negotiation, not a rejection of either principle.

What if my master bedroom cannot face the south-west? The south-west corner is typically considered favourable for the master bedroom. On a plot where this placement conflicts with the overall logic of the floor plan, we explore alternatives: the position of the bed within the room, the orientation of the head while sleeping, and whether the room's character and light quality can compensate for the directional constraint. These adjustments satisfy the underlying intent in most cases.

What if my plot does not face the right direction? The orientation of the plot is fixed before we arrive. Our job is to make the best possible design within that constraint. Most Vastu guidelines are about the internal organisation of the home, not about the plot direction, and there is more room to work with than most people assume when they first raise the question.

When a Vastu guideline genuinely cannot be followed

On some projects, particularly on narrow urban plots in Gujarat where the site geometry dictates the floor plan more than ideal orientation does, certain Vastu requirements simply cannot be met without compromising the structural logic of the building or significantly reducing its livability. In these cases, we are transparent with clients and their families. We explain the constraint clearly, we present the alternatives we have considered, and we let the family make an informed choice together. Many families find that a thoughtfully designed home that addresses 80 percent of their Vastu priorities is far more satisfying to live in than a technically compliant floor plan that does not function well for their daily life.

If you are navigating Vastu considerations alongside a new home or renovation project and want to discuss how to balance them, speak to us at VOAD. We have worked through these questions many times and are glad to help you find the right balance for your specific site and family.
author: Ar. Vivek Bosmiya

title: Architect or Interior Designer: Which One Do You Actually Need?
excerpt: The two titles are often used interchangeably, but the roles are genuinely different. Here is a clear explanation of what each professional does, where they overlap, and when you need both.
content:
We are asked this question often, and it is a good one. The titles get used interchangeably in common conversation, and in parts of India the practical distinction is not always visible to the person hiring. Choosing the wrong type of professional for your project, or hiring one when you actually need both, costs time and sometimes money.

Here is a clear explanation of what each role actually covers, where they overlap, and how to decide which professional, or combination of professionals, your project needs.

What an architect is qualified to do

In India, a registered architect has completed a five-year professional degree and is registered with the Council of Architecture. Architects are legally permitted to sign and submit drawings to municipal authorities for building approvals. They are trained in structural systems, building services such as electrical, plumbing, and HVAC, fire safety standards, accessibility requirements, and the technical aspects of construction from foundation to roof.

If you are building a new home from the ground up, or making structural changes to an existing one, adding a floor, removing load-bearing walls, or changing the building footprint, you need a registered architect involved. Architects are also trained to think about how a building performs on its specific site: its orientation relative to the sun and prevailing wind, its relationship to neighbouring buildings, its thermal behaviour across different seasons. These decisions shape how the building works for decades.

What an interior designer is qualified to do

An interior designer focuses on the experience of the internal space. This covers space planning and furniture layouts, material selection for floors, walls, and ceilings, lighting design, colour and texture, furniture specification, and the overall atmosphere of the interior environment. A trained interior designer will often hold a degree in interior design or a related field, but they are not necessarily registered architects and are typically not authorised to submit structural drawings for municipal approvals.

Interior design is also a broad field with genuine specialisations. The skills and sensibility required for a luxury private home are quite different from those needed for a boutique restaurant, a corporate office, or a retail space. When hiring, look for a portfolio that demonstrates relevant experience in the type of project you are planning, not just impressive work in a different category.

Where the two roles overlap in practice

In India, many architecture studios, including VOAD, practice both architecture and interior design as a continuous service. This is common and practical: the transition from designing a building to designing its interior environment is a natural one when the same studio handles both. The alternative, where the architect and interior designer are different people working in sequence, requires careful coordination to avoid decisions that conflict with each other, particularly around structural element positions, services routing, and the location of fixed joinery.

At VOAD, Ar. Vivek Bosmiya works across both disciplines, which means the design thinking is continuous from the building's structure to the finish of the floor you walk on. There is no hand-off between the architectural and interior phase, no coordination gap, and no moment where the interior design has to work around architectural decisions it was not part of.

When you need an architect, when you need an interior designer, and when you need both

For new construction or structural renovation, you need a registered architect. For interior fit-out of an existing space without structural changes, an interior designer can lead the project, with technical input from an architect on specific matters if needed. For projects that involve both building work and interior specification, a studio that offers both services under one roof will typically deliver a more coherent result and require less coordination effort from the client.

The questions people ask most often

Can my interior designer prepare my building plans? In India, only a Council of Architecture-registered architect can sign and submit plans for municipal approval. An interior designer may be skilled at space planning within an existing structure but cannot legally submit new building drawings unless they hold an architecture qualification and registration. Ask directly about this before hiring.

Can my architect choose my furniture and finishes? Many architects in India also handle interior design, but not all architects are comfortable with or trained in the detailed decisions of material sourcing, furniture specification, and finish selection. Ask specifically whether interior design is included in the architect's scope, and what that scope covers in practice.

Do I genuinely need both? For most residential projects that involve building new or making substantial structural changes, you benefit most from a studio where architecture and interior design are handled together from the start. If you want to talk through which approach suits your specific project, speak to us at VOAD. We are happy to advise without any obligation on your part.
author: Ar. Vivek Bosmiya

title: What We Think About Before Drawing a Single Line
excerpt: The thinking that happens before the first drawing is the most important work in any architecture or interior design project. Here is what that process actually looks like at VOAD.
content:
Every project at VOAD begins the same way. A conversation. A site visit. A long, unhurried look at the people who are going to live or work in the space we are about to design. All of this happens before a single line is drawn, and that is entirely deliberate.

Architecture and interior design are often presented as visual disciplines. And they are, eventually. But the decisions that make a space genuinely comfortable to live in are almost never visual decisions first. They are decisions about how people actually use rooms, how light moves across a site in June compared to December, and what a family wants their home to feel like in ten years, not just in the first week after they move in.

Start with the brief, not the mood board

The brief is the foundation of the whole project, and a good one takes time to develop. We spend the first meeting asking questions rather than showing references. How does this family actually wake up in the morning? Do they eat formally or informally? Is the kitchen a private workspace or the social centre of the home? Are there elderly parents who will need ground-floor access in the years ahead? Are there young children who need to be visible from the cooking area while a parent is at the stove?

A good brief is not a list of rooms and a square footage. It is an understanding of how real people live, day to day, across all seasons. And it is the document we return to every time a design decision becomes difficult. Before any discussion of materials or colours or lighting layouts, we need to understand the life that the space is meant to hold.

Reading the site before designing the building

Before we produce any drawings, we visit the site multiple times. We measure it precisely, but we also observe it. Where does the morning light fall? How does the plot relate to adjacent buildings and the street? What is the prevailing wind direction? In Gujarat, where summer temperatures regularly exceed 42 degrees Celsius for months at a stretch, the orientation of a home is one of the most important decisions in the entire design. A living area facing west in Rajkot is a fundamentally different design problem from a north-facing one, and solving it correctly from the start is far cheaper than managing the consequence with air conditioning and heavy curtains for the next 30 years.

Designing for the family, not the photograph

We ask clients to show us how they use their current home. Not their aspirations, but their actual habits. The sofa that everyone really sits on versus the formal chairs that nobody uses. The bedroom that became a study when the second child arrived. The kitchen island that turned into the homework table every evening. These patterns tell us far more about what a new home genuinely needs than any reference image from a magazine does.

The most successful homes we have worked on are the ones where the design came from a clear understanding of the specific family. Not from a trend. Not from what looked good in a render. From an honest reading of how those particular people actually live their lives.

Aligning the brief with the budget honestly

One of the most important conversations we have with every client is about money, and we have it early. Not to limit what is possible, but to align expectations before anything is designed. The worst version of a project is one that falls short of what the client wanted because the gap between the brief and the budget was never properly discussed.

In our experience, most residential projects in India begin with a mental budget that sits 20 to 30 percent below what the brief actually calls for. This is not a problem when it is identified at the start. It is simply a design challenge: perhaps fewer rooms at a higher quality specification, or a phased approach that delivers the core project now with scope to add later. Both can produce excellent results. What cannot produce a good result is discovering the gap halfway through construction, when materials are already ordered and walls are already standing.

Why we do not rush to drawings

There is pressure in this industry to show clients something visual quickly. Mood boards in the first week, renders before the site has been properly measured. We understand why this is reassuring. Visuals make a project feel real. But they can also create a premature commitment to a direction that has not yet been fully thought through.

We prefer to take the time to think carefully at the beginning, even when it means the client waits a little longer to see anything on paper. The time invested in the brief, in observing the site, and in understanding the family's lifestyle pays back many times over in fewer revisions, fewer surprises on site, and a result that genuinely serves the people living in it.

The invisible work that shapes the visible result

By the time we sit down to produce the first floor plan, most of the consequential decisions have already been made. The orientation of the main living spaces. The relationship between public and private areas of the home. The sizes of rooms tested against how the family actually uses space. The position of service areas relative to the rest of the home. The approach to natural light and ventilation across Gujarat's seasons.

A visitor who walks into a well-designed home simply feels that it is right. The rooms are neither too large nor too small. The light falls where it should. The circulation makes intuitive sense. That feeling is the product of careful thinking that happened before anything was visible. The first conversation costs nothing and shapes everything that follows.
